## Write down the current state before changing it

The single habit that has saved the most time, across every environment I've worked in, is writing down what a system currently does — and why — before changing it. It sounds slower. It almost never is, because it forces a real understanding of the system before touching it, and it gives every future troubleshooting session a starting point that isn't guesswork.

## A rollback plan is part of the change, not an afterthought

If a change doesn't have a written way to undo it, it isn't ready to make yet. This is true whether the change takes five minutes or five weeks — the size of the change doesn't change whether it needs a way back.

## Documentation is for the next person, who is often you

Six months later, the person reading a runbook or a change log has usually forgotten the context that felt obvious at the time. Writing for that future reader — explicit about assumptions, not just steps — is what makes documentation actually useful instead of just present.

## Simple and current beats thorough and stale

A short document that stays accurate is worth more than an exhaustive one that quietly drifts out of date. Documentation that isn't updated as part of the change itself becomes actively misleading faster than having no documentation at all.

## This is the throughline across two decades of very different roles

From a first customer-service job through infrastructure automation today, the roles have changed completely — the discipline of understanding before acting, and writing it down, hasn't.
